summary: Iran lies in West Asia. Anciently known as Persia, it gave rise to ancient empires such as the Achaemenid Empire, and became an Islamic Republic after the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

ranking.name: Islam (Shia)
ranking.description: In 1501 the Safavid dynasty made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion. Through forced conversion and by importing Shia scholars from Lebanon and Iraq, it turned Persia from a mostly Sunni land into a Shia country, distinguishing it from the Sunni Ottoman Empire. After the 1979 Islamic Revolution, Shia clerics took supreme power through the system of "guardianship of the Islamic jurist" (velayat-e faqih); the holy cities of Qom and Mashhad are the religious centers.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: When the Safavid dynasty pushed Shiaization, some peoples in the peripheral regions kept their original Sunni faith, so Sunnis today are concentrated mainly among the Baluch in the southeast, the Kurds in the west and the Turkmen in the northeast. Under a Shia-dominated regime, their religious posts and mosque construction are often restricted.

ranking.name: Other
ranking.description: This includes Zoroastrianism, the ancient pre-Islamic religion (concentrated in Yazd and Kerman), the long-established Jewish community, Armenian and Assyrian Christians, and the Baha'i Faith, which arose in Iran in the 19th century. The first three have guaranteed seats in parliament, while the Baha'i Faith is not recognized and has suffered severe persecution since 1979.

religion.background: In ancient times Iran had Zoroastrianism as its state religion. After Arab Muslims defeated the Sasanian Empire in the mid-7th century, Islam gradually replaced Zoroastrianism over several centuries, and most people at that time were Sunni. In 1501 Ismail I of the Safavid dynasty established Twelver Shia Islam as the state religion and enforced conversion, making Iran the world's largest Shia country. After the 1979 Islamic Revolution, Khomeini founded an "Islamic Republic" supervised by clerics, in which religion and politics are closely fused. The constitution recognizes Zoroastrianism, Judaism and Christianity as protected minority religions, while the Baha'i Faith has long been persecuted.

ranking.name: Persian
ranking.description: New Persian became Iran's literary and administrative language from the 9th century. In the 20th century the Pahlavi dynasty pursued centralization and made Persian the sole language of schools and the media. Thus, although native speakers make up only about half the population, almost all Iranians know Persian, and it is the common national language of all ethnic groups.

ranking.name: Azerbaijani
ranking.description: From the 11th century, Turkic tribes such as the Seljuks entered northwestern Iran, and the local population gradually switched to speaking Turkic, forming the Azerbaijani language. After the Russo-Persian War that ended in 1828, the Azerbaijan region was split in two: the north went to Russia (today's Republic of Azerbaijan) and the south remained in Iran. As a result, Azerbaijanis in Iran outnumber even those in Azerbaijan itself, and are concentrated around Tabriz.

ranking.name: Kurdish
ranking.description: Kurdish belongs to the Iranian branch of languages and shares a common origin with Persian; its speakers are the Kurds living in the Zagros Mountains. In the 16th century the Ottoman and Safavid empires drew a border, dividing the Kurds among present-day Turkey, Iraq, Syria and Iran. Iran's Kurds are concentrated in the western provinces of Kurdistan, Kermanshah and others.

ranking.name: Arabic
ranking.description: After the 7th-century Arab conquest, Arab tribes migrated into southwestern Iran, and today's Arabic speakers live mainly in Khuzestan Province, near Iraq. In addition, Arabic, as the language of the Quran, is a compulsory subject in Iranian schools.

language.history: Persian is a language of the Iranian branch of the Indo-European family. Old Persian appears in the cuneiform inscriptions of the 6th-century BCE Achaemenid Empire, and Middle Persian (Pahlavi) was used in the Sasanian period. After the Arab conquest, New Persian, written in the Arabic script and absorbing many Arabic words, arose in the 9th–10th centuries. The epic Shahnameh (Book of Kings), completed by Ferdowsi around 1010, deliberately used few Arabic words and is regarded as a milestone in preserving the Persian language and national identity. Persian was once the cultural language of the courts of Central Asia, the Ottomans and Mughal India. In the 20th century the Pahlavi dynasty enforced a policy making Persian the sole national language, and minority languages such as Azerbaijani and Kurdish were long restricted in education.

ranking.name: Chelow kabab (rice with kebab)
ranking.description: White rice (chelow) served with skewers of grilled minced meat or chunks of grilled meat, accompanied by grilled tomato, butter, raw egg yolk and sumac. The rice is often mixed with butter and saffron; it is the most common restaurant dish in Iran.
ranking.history: Chelow kabab is generally thought to have become popular in the Tehran bazaars during the Qajar dynasty in the 19th century; restaurants serving the dish are said to have existed already in the time of Naser al-Din Shah. Iranians have long prized the skill of boiling and steaming rice, and paired with grilled meat that comes from the Turkic nomadic tradition, it became the most representative restaurant dish. Today it is often called Iran's "national dish" and is also common at weddings and festivals.

ranking.name: Ghormeh sabzi (herb stew)
ranking.description: Large amounts of herbs such as leek, parsley, coriander and fenugreek leaves are sauteed, then slow-cooked with lamb, red kidney beans and dried limes, and served with white rice.
ranking.history: Ghormeh sabzi means "stewed herbs", and its history is generally thought to go back several centuries or more. Iranian stews (khoresh) prize sourness and aroma, and the dried lime (limoo amani) comes from the Persian Gulf coast, reflecting trade with places such as Oman. Many Iranians regard it as the dish that tastes most of home, and Iranian communities abroad often cook it at gatherings to remember their homeland.

ranking.name: Fesenjān (pomegranate walnut chicken stew)
ranking.description: Chicken or duck stewed in ground walnuts and pomegranate molasses, giving a dark brown, sweet-and-sour, rich sauce. It is usually eaten with white rice, and the sauce must be simmered for hours to thicken.
ranking.history: Fesenjān originated around Gilan Province on Iran's northern Caspian coast, where pomegranates, walnuts and wild ducks abound. Iranian cuisine has long favored cooking with fruit to create interwoven sweet and sour flavors, and fesenjān is representative of this ancient taste tradition. Laborious and made with costly ingredients, it often appears at feasts such as weddings and Yalda Night (the winter solstice).

ranking.name: Tahdig (crispy rice)
ranking.description: When cooking Iranian rice, a golden, crispy crust is deliberately formed at the bottom of the pot, sometimes layered with potato slices, flatbread or saffron yogurt rice. It is crisp and fragrant, and is usually turned out whole onto a platter and then cut up.
ranking.history: Iranians cook rice by first boiling and then steaming it (polow), and the rice at the bottom of the pot is fried by the oil and heat into crispy tahdig (meaning "bottom of the pot"). In Iranian households it is regarded as the most precious part of the meal, and people at the table often compete for it; when a host shares the crust with guests it also signifies warm hospitality. This method has spread abroad with Iranian emigrants and has attracted attention in Western food circles in recent years.

ranking.name: Ash reshteh (noodle soup)
ranking.description: A thick soup made with noodles, chickpeas, lentils, beans and plenty of herbs, topped with fried onions, mint oil and fermented whey (kashk).
ranking.history: Ash in Persian refers to thick soups in general, and in ancient times it even gave rise to the word for "cook" (ashpaz, one who makes soup), showing the place of soup in Iranian food culture. The noodles (reshteh) in ash reshteh symbolize "grasping the threads of life", so it is often cooked before the Nowruz new year or when relatives and friends set off on a journey, to pray for good luck. It is also common at the breaking of the fast during Ramadan and in winter, and is one of Iran's most widespread commoner soups.
